pipeline.attack_summary: Slingshot is an advanced APT that compromises Mikrotik routers via Winbox Loader, placing malicious DLLs like ipv4.dll to download additional components. It uses kernel-mode modules such as Cahnadr/NDriver and GollumApp for persistence, data collection, and C2 communication, leveraging vulnerable drivers for privilege escalation.

indicators.context: This is the name of the malicious loader internally named 'Slingshot', part of a new, and highly sophisticated attack platform.
The initial loader replaces the victim's legitimate Windows library 'scesrv.dll' with a malicious one of exactly the same size.
One of them – ipv4.dll – has been placed by the APT with what is, in fact, a downloader for other malicious components.

The most sophisticated module is GollumApp. This contains nearly 1,500 user-code functions and provides most of the above described routines for persistence, file system control and C&C communications. Canhadr, also known as NDriver, contains low-level routines for network, IO operations and so on.

The most sophisticated module is GollumApp. This contains nearly 1,500 user-code functions and provides most of the above described routines for persistence, file system control and C&C communications.
Canhadr, also known as NDriver, contains low-level routines for network, IO operations and so on.
During our research we also found a component called KPWS that turned out to be another downloader for Slingshot components.

In turn, this infected the administrator of the router. We believe that most of the victims we observed appeared to have been initially infected through a Windows exploit or compromised Mikrotik routers. The exact method used by Slingshot to exploit the routers in the first instance is not yet clear. When the target user runs Winbox Loader software (a utility used for Mikrotik router configuration), this connects to the router and downloads some DLLs (dynamic link libraries) from the router’s file system.
These vulnerabilities include CVE-2007-5633; CVE-2010-1592, CVE-2009-0824.

I know the Technicolor TC8717T Wireless Telephony DOCSIS 3.0 Modem, 4 Port Router which comes with ISP Xfinity, has been harnessed this attack.
The earliest sample we found was compiled in 2012 and the threat was still active in February 2018.

The malware uses COM hijacking for persistence by modifying registry keys pointing to malicious DLLs in the Windows IME folders. It employs DLL hijacking via 'windows.old\windows' path and modifies registry under CLSID to load malicious DLL. The malware communicates with C2 domains such as msstore[.]io, adtracker[.]link, and cdnmobile[.]io.

pipeline.attack_summary: The attack begins with unauthenticated access to Veeam Backup & Replication via TCP port 9401 using CVE-2023-27532, followed by SQL shell command execution that triggers in-memory download and execution of a PowerShell script named POWERTRASH. The threat actor then performs reconnaissance, credential theft, and establishes persistence using custom scripts like gup18.ps1 and DUBLOADER, which leverages a malicious libcurl.dll to execute DICELOADER. Lateral movement is achieved through WMI and SMB, with command-and-control communication over port 443.

indicators.context: An SQL server process related to the Veeam Backup instance executed a shell command
The script contains an embedded payload that is executed through reflective PE injection. POWERTRASH is an obfuscated loader written in PowerShell that has been attributed to FIN7
The filenames (e.g. icsnd16_64refl.ps1, icbt11801_64refl.ps1) used for these PowerShell scripts were also (notably) identical to the naming convention reportedly used by FIN7
The filenames (e.g. icsnd16_64refl.ps1, icbt11801_64refl.ps1) used for these PowerShell scripts were also (notably) identical to the naming convention reportedly used by FIN7

A custom PowerShell script, "gup18.ps1", was executed to set up an active foothold in the compromised machine by creating a persistence mechanism to execute DICELOADER on device startup

The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, into a unique folder in %APPDATA%, and sets an autorun registry entry to establish persistence. The dropped files include gup.exe – Legitimate GUP.exe binary (part of the Notepad++ application)

The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, into a unique folder in %APPDATA%, and sets an autorun registry entry to establish persistence. The dropped files include gup.xml – Configuration file that’s part of the GUP application
libcurl.dll – .NET DLL file side-loaded by gup.exe
JZ4qWKZW – Encoded DICELOADER payload that’s loaded and executed by libcurl.dll
jkBDfXaL.bat – Batch file that executes gup.exe
0JNvHvAz.vbs – VBScript file that executes the batch file

An additional file called "host_ip.ps1" was dropped and executed on the compromised Veeam backup servers. The PowerShell script content is nearly identical to a code snippet shared online for resolving IP to Hostname with PowerShell

An additional file called "445.ps1" was dropped and executed on the compromised Veeam backup servers. The retrieved script content functions as a port checker, which tests whether a port is open for a given address by attempting to establish a socket connection
This script performed remote injection into the ‘PlugPlay’ service, which made a network connection to a remote host on port 443

The threat actor used a series of commands as well as custom scripts to gather host and network information from the compromised machines. Some of these commands included: netstat  : Display all active TCP connections and listening ports

The threat actor used a series of commands as well as custom scripts to gather host and network information from the compromised machines. Some of these commands included: tasklist  : Display all running processes

The threat actor used a series of commands as well as custom scripts to gather host and network information from the compromised machines. Some of these commands included: ipconfig : Display all IP configurations

This script was hosted on an external file-hosting service "temp[.]sh". This unique PowerShell script has not been previously seen in the attack arsenal of FIN7, and we are now tracking it as POWERHOLD

The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, into a unique folder in %APPDATA%, and sets an autorun registry entry to establish persistence. The dropped files include JZ4qWKZW – Encoded DICELOADER payload that’s loaded and executed by libcurl.dll

The crafted loader is designed to mimic the legitimate libcurl.dll file by including export function names found in the legitimate version and thus imported by the GUP executable. Only one of the export functions, namely "curl_easy_init" contains malicious code. All other export functions are trivially implemented with "retn 0" instructions. The "curl_easy_init" export function, which implements the malicious code, is the first function[9] from the library that is called by the GUP executable. Therefore, the malicious code is executed immediately when GUP.exe is launched. This unique loader has not been previously seen in FIN7’s attack arsenal, and we are now tracking it as DUBLOADER

The 'class.module.classLoader' pattern in selection_ognl is a strong indicator but may also appear in legitimate scripts using classloader access. Consider adding additional context or filtering to reduce false positives.
The 'System.setProperty' pattern in selection_privilege could generate false positives from legitimate system configuration scripts. Additional filtering may be needed.
